I'll solve this directly. Let me analyze the integral by examining the singular regions.

## Proof

We determine for which $p \in \mathbb{R}$ (with $n \geq 1$) the integral
$$I(p) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \bigl|\log|x|\bigr|^p\,dx$$
converges. The integrand is nonnegative, so convergence is absolute, and we may use polar coordinates. Writing $r = |x|$ and $\omega \in S^{n-1}$, we have $dx = r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\omega$, so
$$I(p) = |S^{n-1}|\int_0^\infty \bigl|\log r\bigr|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr.$$
The integrand has three regions of concern: $r \to 0^+$, $r \to 1$ (where $\log r = 0$), and $r \to \infty$. The full integral converges only if **all three** regional integrals converge.

---

**Region 1: near $r = 0$ (say $0 < r < \tfrac12$).** Here $\log r < 0$, so $|\log r| = -\log r = \log(1/r)$. Substitute $u = \log(1/r)$, so $r = e^{-u}$, $dr = -e^{-u}\,du$:
$$\int_0^{1/2} |\log r|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr = \int_{\log 2}^{\infty} u^p\,e^{-u(n-1)}\,e^{-u}\,du = \int_{\log 2}^{\infty} u^p\,e^{-nu}\,du.$$
The exponential $e^{-nu}$ (with $n \geq 1$) dominates any power $u^p$, so this integral **converges for every $p \in \mathbb{R}$**.

---

**Region 2: near $r = 1$ (say $\tfrac12 < r < 2$).** Here $|\log r|$ vanishes at $r=1$. For $p \geq 0$, $|\log r|^p$ is bounded (indeed continuous after setting value $0$ at $r=1$), so the integral over this compact annulus converges. For $p < 0$, write $q = -p > 0$; then $|\log r|^p = 1/|\log r|^q$ blows up at $r=1$. Since $\log r = (r-1) + O((r-1)^2)$ near $r=1$, we have $|\log r| \sim |r-1|$, hence
$$|\log r|^p \sim |r-1|^p \quad (r \to 1).$$
The integral $\int_{1/2}^{2}|r-1|^p\,dr$ converges if and only if $p > -1$. The smooth bounded factor $r^{n-1}$ does not change this threshold. Thus Region 2 converges **iff $p > -1$**.

---

**Region 3: near infinity (say $r > 2$).** Here $\log r > 0$, so $|\log r|^p = (\log r)^p$. We claim
$$J(p) = \int_2^{\infty}(\log r)^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr = +\infty \quad\text{for every }p\in\mathbb{R},\ n\geq 1.$$

- If $p \geq 0$: then $(\log r)^p \geq 1$ for $r \geq e$, and $r^{n-1} \geq 1$ for $r \geq 1$ (since $n \geq 1$), so $J(p) \geq \int_e^\infty 1\,dr = +\infty$.

- If $p < 0$: write $q = -p > 0$, so the integrand is $r^{n-1}/(\log r)^q$. For $r$ large, $\log r \leq r^{1/(2q)}$ (since logarithm grows slower than any positive power), hence $(\log r)^q \leq r^{1/2}$, giving
$$\frac{r^{n-1}}{(\log r)^q} \geq \frac{r^{n-1}}{r^{1/2}} = r^{n - 3/2}.$$
  For $n \geq 2$, $n - 3/2 \geq 1/2 > -1$, so $\int r^{n-3/2}\,dr$ diverges, hence $J(p) = +\infty$. For $n = 1$, the integrand is $1/(\log r)^q$; since $(\log r)^q \leq r$ for large $r$, we get $1/(\log r)^q \geq 1/r$, and $\int_e^\infty (1/r)\,dr = +\infty$, so $J(p) = +\infty$ as well.

(Equivalently, for $n=1$ the substitution $u = \log r$ gives $J(p) = \int_{\log 2}^{\infty} u^p e^u\,du = +\infty$ for every $p$.) Thus **Region 3 diverges for every $p \in \mathbb{R}$**.

---

**Conclusion.** Since the integral over the exterior region $\{|x| > 2\}$ diverges for every real $p$ (for every $n \geq 1$), the full integral
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl|\log|x|\bigr|^p\,dx$$
**diverges for every $p \in \mathbb{R}$**. The set of values of $p$ for which the integral converges is **empty**.

(For completeness: the only obstruction is at infinity; the origin is harmless for all $p$, and the sphere $|x|=1$ is harmless precisely when $p > -1$—but the divergence at infinity already rules out every $p$.)
